The Story of Incorrect Word Division

I bow to Lord Jina's feet, and I write a story without proper word division, illustrating the importance of correct interpretation.

This story is from the time when Veersen was king of Rajgriha, the capital of Magadh. Veersen's queen was Veersena. They had a son named Singh. King Veersen appointed the Brahmin Somsharma to teach Singh. Somsharma was a good scholar in all subjects.

King Sinhrath of Podanapur had been enemies with Veersen for many days. Seizing the opportunity, Veersen launched an attack on him. From there, Veersen sent a letter regarding state administration to his own capital. Among other news, Veersen had written this sentence about Prince Singh's education: 'Simhoddhyaapayitavyah' (सिंहोध्यापयितव्य:).

When this letter arrived, a half-educated man read it and thought — the root 'dhye' means to remember or contemplate. Therefore, the meaning is: 'Now the burden of state contemplation should be placed on the prince.' He should no longer be taught. The matter was that by dividing the sentence into separate words — 'Simhah adhyapayitavyah' (सिंह:अध्यापयितव्य:) — the meaning is 'Singh should be taught.' But that half-educated letter-reader, understanding the words as 'Simhah dhyaapayitavya' (सिंह:ध्यापयितव्य), did not pay attention to the connecting vowel and, taking only the meaning of 'contemplation' from the root 'dhyai,' stopped the prince's education entirely.

According to grammar, both word divisions are possible and both are correct, but here grammar alone was not enough. Some experience was also needed. Due to the lack of this experience in the letter-reader, he stopped the prince's education. The result was that when the king returned and saw that the prince's education had been stopped, he investigated the cause. Upon learning the true matter, he was very angry at that half-educated, foolish letter-reader. He gave him a very severe punishment for this foolishness.

From this story, worthy souls should learn this lesson: they should never commit such negligence that causes harm to their work in any way. Just as no benefit comes from medicine without proper ingredients — it cannot cure any disease of the body — so too, scriptures or mantras without proper letters (akshar) bring no benefit.

This story teaches the critical importance of correct interpretation and the danger of half-knowledge. The letter-reader, though able to read, lacked the experience and wisdom to properly understand the king's intention. His incorrect interpretation led to the prince's education being stopped, which was a grave matter. The wise should ensure they fully understand instructions before acting on them, and should seek clarification when in doubt. Half-knowledge is more dangerous than no knowledge at all.
